rv.q: Paradise Square is the kind of new musical that Broadway needs more of: an original story that is ambitious, moving and entertaining
The show genuinely wants to be entertaining, of course, and much of the time it succeeds.
It’s the kind of moment that sends electricity up and down your spine as it takes place.
And somewhere along the line it reaches a point of no return, when all that reaching just wears itself out.
The problem is that the writing doesn't support the spectacle, yielding a ponderous hash of good intentions that often feels like a training-wheels version of Ragtime.
The musical's ambitions are admirable, but 'Paradise Square' is a show that never quite finds its footing
Racism becomes an individual character flaw instead of a systemic evil; resistance, the solitary moral genius of a hero.
It makes the virtuosic Black dancers seem unmusical — but really it’s the musical itself failing to listen.

The new musical 'Paradise Square' has ambitions as grand as its sprawling cast and period setting, but despite moments of genuine power, it never quite coheres into the unified artistic statement it strives to be.
Joaquina Kalukango whose memorable performance is certain to go down in the record books and be a top contender for the Tony Award makes this a must-see show.
Paradise Square is an ambitious musical that tackles issues of race, class, and immigration in Civil War-era New York with impressive performances and stunning choreography.
The resilience demonstrated by Kalukango’s character and others in Paradise Square seems fitting in a show that might have been prematurely written off as the latest big musical that couldn’t.
Is this the next Phantom or Les Miserables?
Paradise Square, with its thrilling vocals, virtuosic choreography, and brash declaration of American values, is a bona fide crowd-pleaser.
Challenging, adult shows like this are always welcome but, having gone through a lengthy development process, its overcrowded book still needs sorting out.
Unfortunately, she cannot singlehandedly save a Broadway musical suffering from an identity crisis.
The performances under his direction are scattered all over the Broadway map, from Kalukango’s star-making turn to Dossett’s understated villain to Kennedy’s brassy performance.
Ultimately, there are just too many proverbial “round holes” to comfortably fit into this “Square” peg!
And yet, without a story line to guide us, and songs that do not further the tale, in the end we are left wandering in the wilderness holding a bowlful of good intentions.
Hard Times definitely had its flaws, as my review noted, but it was delightfully appealing, nicely unified, and was much tightly rendered than its grown-up Broadway offspring.
The mechanics of the show work against it.
Paradise Square is a musical that wears its good intentions on its sleeve, but those intentions don't always translate into compelling theater.
Paradise Square is a show that wants to be everything to everyone, and in trying to do so, it ends up being not quite enough for anyone.
But “Paradise Square” was largely a disappointment.
Although well-meaning and filled with some striking visuals and pointed political commentary, “Paradise Square” is sappy, overstuffed, overlong, and tiresome.
For me, it was especially impactful to see the concrete proof that this story is still playing out today, and, therefore, this story is more than just beautiful. It is necessary.
The highlight of the show is without a doubt 'Let it Burn,' Kalukango's 11 o'clock number, which receives a standing ovation and will be canonized alongside the greats.
His work, since he arrived on these shores, has enriched New York and the debut on Broadway of his “Paradise Square” is just what the theater needs to regain its glorious past.
At its best, that variety of contributors have made for a rich, dialectical depiction of a complex slice of history.
The company is continually immersed in song and movement, and the result is a vibrant tableau of a dynamic time in our history.
Neither Paradise Square nor Suffs is truly bad. But neither is as rewarding as it might have been either.

cn.t: Critics find Paradise Square an ambitious but overstuffed musical about Civil War-era New York, praising Joaquina Kalukango's powerhouse performance and Bill T. Jones's thrilling choreography while faulting its sprawling, unfocused book.

sg.ra: TickPick and Headout both name Center Orchestra rows E-J (TickPick: E-J; SeatPlan/Headout: F-O) as the prime zone at the Barrymore because the 1,058-seat house is shallow enough that the mezzanine overhang only kicks in at row K of the orchestra, leaving center rows F-J with an uncovered, forward sightline well-suited to the text-driven plays this house tends to book.

Headout and TickPick both warn against Orchestra rows A-C at the Barrymore specifically because the stage at this 1928 house sits high relative to the front rows — TickPick: 'rows A, B, and C are too close to the stage and might block your view'; Headout adds that 'seats closer to the stage may cause neck strain from looking upward.'

SeatPlan and TickPick both confirm the Barrymore mezzanine overhang begins at row K of the orchestra but isn't obstructive — SeatPlan: 'those sitting in the rear of the Orchestra section will notice that the stage feels impressively close'; the house's well-raked orchestra keeps sightlines intact even under cover, which matters because this is a 1,058-seat intimate-play house and losing the rear orchestra would shrink the good-seat pool significantly.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, under premium pricing
sg.ra: SeatPlan directly names row A Center Front Mezzanine as the house favorite at the Barrymore — 'very popular thanks to its fantastic elevated position above the stage' — and both SeatPlan and TickPick emphasize the Barrymore's front mezzanine is only 5 rows deep (A-E, 196 seats), so even row E retains a wide, pitched view and benefits from the intimate 1,058-seat scale.

SeatPlan specifically praises the Barrymore rear mezzanine rake: 'a decent rake means even the back rows offer a surprisingly good look at the stage' and 'even in the far corner theatergoers won't feel too much strain to make out the stage.' The house's three-flights-up rear mezz is the trade-off for the small footprint, but the rake compensates for distance in a way deeper houses don't manage.

Headout and TickPick both flag the Barrymore's six box seats (three per side of the orchestra) and the orchestra rows D-E directly beneath them as compromised — Headout: 'seats under the Boxes in rows D and E a little restricted'; TickPick adds 'far Left and Right Orchestra and the outer corners of the Mezzanine can have reduced sightlines.' This is a specific quirk of the Barrymore's 1928 proscenium layout with built-in side boxes.
